EXCERPT from the Supreme Court of Nigeria judgment in Ukeje v Ukeje (2014) 11 NWLR (Pt 1418) 384:

'The question for determination in this appeal is whether the Igbo customary law which disinherits a female child from her father's estate is consistent with the provisions of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. The appellant, a female child of the deceased, was excluded from her father's estate on the ground that under Igbo customary law, only male children are entitled to inherit. The trial court and the Court of Appeal upheld this position. The appellant further appealed to this court.

This court has held in a number of decisions that any custom which is repugnant to natural justice, equity and good conscience is not enforceable. Furthermore, section 42(1) of the 1999 Constitution provides that a citizen of Nigeria of a particular community shall not, by reason only of his or her sex, be subjected to any disabilities or restrictions. The Igbo customary law that disinherits female children is a clear violation of this constitutional provision. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The said customary law is declared void to the extent of its inconsistency with the Constitution.'

Based on this excerpt, identify: (1) the ratio decidendi of the case; (2) whether the court made any obiter dicta; and (3) what precedent the case establishes for other customary laws in Nigeria.
dataset.target:
(1) Ratio decidendi: The Igbo customary law that disinherits female children from their father's estate is unconstitutional because it violates section 42(1) of the Constitution, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of sex. The ratio is binding authority throughout Nigeria.

(2) Obiter dicta: The court's reference to 'any custom which is repugnant to natural justice, equity and good conscience is not enforceable' is obiter — it is a general statement of law not necessary for the decision, since the court decided the case on constitutional grounds, not the repugnancy doctrine.

(3) Precedent: The case establishes that any customary law rule that discriminates on the basis of sex is void for inconsistency with section 42 of the Constitution. This applies to all customary laws across Nigeria — not only Igbo inheritance customs but also Yoruba, Hausa, Bini, and other customs that discriminate on the basis of sex. The case is binding on all courts in Nigeria.
dataset.source: Ukeje v Ukeje (2014) 11 NWLR (Pt 1418) 384; Constitution of Nigeria 1999, s. 42

dataset.input:
EXCERPT from the Supreme Court of Nigeria judgment in Ilori v Ishola (2018) 15 NWLR (Pt 1641) 77:

'The appellants contended that the agreement of sale between the parties was void ab initio because the Governor's consent under section 22(1) of the Land Use Act was not obtained before the agreement was executed. The respondent argued that the agreement was expressed to be 'subject to the consent of the Governor' and therefore did not contravene the Act.

This court has held in Savannah Bank v Ajilo that the Governor's consent is mandatory for any alienation of a statutory right of occupancy. However, the question here is different: does section 22(1) prohibit the holder of a statutory right of occupancy from entering into an agreement to alienate, where such agreement is explicitly subject to the Governor's consent? We hold that it does not. Section 22(1) prohibits actual alienation without consent, not negotiation subject to consent. The agreement in this case was not a completed alienation — it was an executory contract conditional upon the Governor's consent being obtained. The appellants, having benefited from the transaction, cannot now approbate and reprobate by claiming the agreement is void. Equity will not permit them to take advantage of their own failure to fulfil the condition of obtaining consent.'

Based on this excerpt, what is the key distinction the Supreme Court draws between this case and Savannah Bank v Ajilo?
dataset.target: The Supreme Court distinguishes between: (a) a completed alienation without consent (which is void under Savannah Bank v Ajilo and section 26 of the Land Use Act); and (b) an executory contract expressed to be 'subject to the Governor's consent' (which is not void but conditional/inchoate). The court holds that section 22(1) prohibits the actual alienation (transfer of title) without consent — it does not prohibit parties from negotiating and signing an agreement that is explicitly conditional on future consent. Such an agreement is not a completed alienation but an executory contract that becomes fully effective only when consent is obtained. The distinction turns on whether the transaction purports to transfer title immediately (void without consent) or whether it merely records the parties' agreement pending consent (enforceable as a conditional contract, though inchoate until consent is obtained).
dataset.source: Ilori v Ishola (2018) 15 NWLR (Pt 1641) 77; Land Use Act, ss. 22(1), 26
